relationships.description: The application service reads, creates or updates the business-level information, such as an order, invoice or contract, that its operations act upon on behalf of consumers.
relationships.evidence: The service's operation signatures or handler code read or persist the entity that the business model documents as that business object, e.g. an OrderService.submit method that writes the Order record.

relationships.description: The application service's operations read, write or transform the code-level data structure as their input, output or working state.
relationships.evidence: The service interface or implementation takes, returns or mutates the class, record or DTO, e.g. a method signature `CustomerDto getCustomer(id)` or repository calls that save that type.

relationships.description: Invocation of the application service is permitted only when the access condition's predicate on a request attribute evaluates to true.
relationships.evidence: A policy file or authorization middleware binds a condition such as `request.tenant == user.tenant` to the service's routes or operations, and calls are rejected when it fails.

relationships.description: Making the application service available produces the worth or benefit that stakeholders recognize as the value, such as faster checkout or reduced manual effort.
relationships.evidence: Product or architecture documentation, business cases or OKR pages attribute the stated value explicitly to the service, ideally backed by a KPI dashboard tied to the service's usage.

relationships.description: The application service cannot fulfil its operations without calling another application service, so the latter's unavailability breaks it.
relationships.evidence: The service's implementation contains client calls, SDK imports or service-mesh configuration targeting the other service's endpoint, and its health check or failure handling reflects that dependency.

relationships.description: The application service requires the data structure to exist and keep its shape in order to function, so changes to the data object break the service contract.
relationships.evidence: The service's API schema or code imports and uses the data object type such that compilation or contract tests fail if the type is removed or altered.

relationships.description: Data or control produced by the source application service is passed on to the destination application service as the next step in an end-to-end interaction.
relationships.evidence: The source service publishes an event, message or response that the destination service consumes, as shown in queue/topic subscriptions, workflow definitions or distributed traces linking the two.

relationships.description: The application service is the automated means through which the business service is actually delivered to its customers.
relationships.evidence: Architecture documentation or service catalog entries map the business service to the application service, and the service's endpoints implement the business service's described operations.

relationships.description: The application service provides the concrete technical behavior that gives the product the stated capability.
relationships.evidence: A capability map or product spec lists the application service as the implementation of the capability, and removing the service would leave the capability unavailable.

relationships.description: The application service supplies the operations that make the user-visible product feature work.
relationships.evidence: The feature's spec, ticket or feature flag is wired to the service's endpoints, e.g. the frontend feature calls the service's API and the feature toggle gates its routes.

relationships.description: The application service is put in place as a concrete means of achieving the stated goal.
relationships.evidence: Architecture decision records or roadmap documentation cite the goal as the rationale for building the service and trace the service to that goal.

relationships.description: The application service provides the behavior that fulfils the stated requirement.
relationships.evidence: A requirements traceability matrix, ticket link or acceptance test maps the requirement ID to the service's operations, and those tests pass against the service.

relationships.description: The application service points to the tracer provider configuration that determines how its spans are sampled, propagated and processed, without depending on it functionally.
relationships.evidence: The service's startup code or config (e.g. OTEL_* environment variables or an otel config file) names that sampler, propagator and span processor setup.

relationships.description: Consumers must be authenticated according to the authentication configuration, identity provider, MFA and session rules, before the application service will handle their calls.
relationships.evidence: The service's security configuration or gateway route declares the identity provider, OIDC/JWT validation or MFA policy, and unauthenticated requests receive 401 responses.

relationships.description: The application service is designed and operated within the limits that the constraint imposes, such as a mandated technology, region or latency budget.
relationships.evidence: Deployment manifests, technology choices or compliance checks for the service demonstrably conform to the constraint, e.g. data-residency settings restricting it to the required region.

relationships.description: The application component consumes the application service's operations to carry out its own responsibilities.
relationships.evidence: The component's code holds a client, injected interface or API call to the service, e.g. a dependency-injected PaymentService used inside the component.

relationships.description: The application function invokes the application service's operations as part of the internal work it performs.
relationships.evidence: The function's implementation calls the service's interface or endpoint, visible as a method call or HTTP/RPC client invocation inside that function's code.

relationships.description: One or more steps of the application process call the application service to obtain the results the sequence needs.
relationships.evidence: The workflow, saga or pipeline definition includes a step that invokes the service's operation, e.g. a Temporal activity or step function task targeting its endpoint.

relationships.description: The application service automates or supports activities within the business process, which uses it to reach its business result.
relationships.evidence: Process documentation or BPMN models show process tasks performed via the service, and the service's API is called from the system that executes those tasks.

relationships.description: The application service is offered for the benefit of the stakeholder, whose interests it is intended to meet.
relationships.evidence: The service catalog, product documentation or SLA names the stakeholder group as the intended consumer or beneficiary of the service.

notes: accesses vs depends-on DataObject overlap. realizes Goal is non-standard; supports/supports-goals fits better. realizes Requirement vs satisfies Constraint use inconsistent predicates for similar traceability. flows-to vs depends-on between services may duplicate. Serving a Stakeholder (motivation element) is odd; serve a role/actor instead. AccessCondition is too fine-grained; constrain via a policy rule.
